bull.argument: Costco's 2026 results show strong momentum. Net sales rose 10% to $297,247 million, and comparable sales grew 8%, with 7% growth excluding gasoline and currency effects, indicating the core business is healthy rather than merely riding fuel prices. Membership fee revenue increased 11% to $5,907 million, and renewal rates held at 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada, a recurring revenue base that supports profitability. Net income grew 14% to $9,226 million, or $20.76 per diluted share, and the Board approved a 13% dividend increase. Digitally-enabled comparable sales rose 21%, showing the model is reaching members beyond the warehouse. Management also flagged the IEEPA tariff refunds as a meaningful tailwind, with $184 million received in 2026 and $155 million more afterward, which management plans to largely return to members as value. The filing's risk factors are real, particularly the heavy dependence on California and the Canadian business, but the reported numbers show growth across segments and a resilient membership model.

claims.claim: Comparable sales grew strongly even excluding gasoline and currency effects.
claims.quote: Increases in comparable sales excluding the impact of changes in foreign-currency and gasoline prices (1) : U.S. 7 % 7 % 5 % Canada 7 % 8 % 8 %

claims.claim: Membership fee revenue grew 11% on a recurring base with high renewal rates.
claims.quote: At the end of 2026, member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.

claims.claim: Net income rose 14% with higher earnings per diluted share.
claims.quote: Net income increased 14% to $9,226, $20.76 per diluted share, compared to $8,099, $18.21 per diluted share in 2025

bear.argument: The bull case rests on growth that is less durable than it appears. Net sales rose 10%, but the filing says higher gasoline prices added $3,501 million, or 130 basis points, and that gasoline volume contributed another $1,913 million. Fuel-driven sales are inherently cyclical and reverse when prices fall. Gross margin percentage fell three basis points to 11.09%, and the filing attributes the mix shift to lower-margin ancillary sales growing faster than core merchandise, which sits 11 basis points lower. Earnings also lean on one-time items: the $184 million in IEEPA tariff refunds was recorded as a reduction to merchandise costs, and management says most will be returned to members, so it is not clearly repeatable. Concentration risk is significant: the U.S. and Canada produced 86% and 83% of net sales and operating income, and California alone is 26% of U.S. sales. Finally, the filing flags heavy IT and AI investment with unproven returns and cybersecurity exposure.

claims.claim: Gasoline prices, not core demand alone, drove a large share of sales growth, and that effect can reverse.
claims.quote: Higher gasoline prices positively impacted net sales by $3,501, or 130 basis points, with a 12% increase in the average price per gallon.

claims.claim: Gross margin percentage declined, and the filing ties the mix shift toward lower-margin ancillary sales to that pressure.
claims.quote: Gross margin percentage decreased three basis points; it increased 10 basis points excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation

claims.claim: Earnings are concentrated in a few regions, with heavy dependence on California.
claims.quote: Within the U.S., we are highly dependent on our California operations, which comprised 26% of U.S. net sales in 2026.

bull.argument: The bear case is fair on fuel and mix, but it understates what the filing shows. Strip out gasoline and currency and comparable sales still rose 7% in the U.S. and Canada, so the core warehouse business is growing, not just riding fuel prices. Gross margin percentage excluding gasoline inflation rose 10 basis points to 11.22%, and management explicitly notes the mix shift toward ancillary sales is what pushed the reported figure down, a timing effect rather than eroding pricing. On the refunds, management itself says they are not treated as earnings to keep: a portion already went to lower prices, and the majority of the remainder is intended for member value. That means the refunds are a pass-through, not a durable profit cushion, so the bear's point cuts against overstating earnings, and the bull case should not rely on them. Membership fees grew 11%, and renewal held at 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada, a recurring base the fuel cycle does not touch. The concentration risk is real, and the filing says so plainly, but the growth is broad across segments, with Other International up 12%. Net income still rose 14%.

claims.claim: Gross margin excluding gasoline inflation increased 10 basis points.
claims.quote: Excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation on net sales, gross margin percentage was 11.22%, an increase of 10 basis points.

claims.claim: Core comparable sales growth held up excluding gasoline and currency effects.
claims.quote: Increases in comparable sales excluding the impact of changes in foreign-currency and gasoline prices (1) : U.S. 7 % 7 % 5 % Canada 7 % 8 % 8 %

claims.claim: Management plans to invest most IEEPA refunds back into member value.
claims.quote: we intend to continue to invest the majority of the refunds in increased value for the member.

bear.argument: The bull's rebuttal leans on figures that the filing itself qualifies. Ex-gasoline comparable sales growth of 7% is real, but the filing shows it fell from 8% in 2025 for the Total Company, and Canada's ex-gasoline comparable sales slowed from 8% to 7%. Gross margin excluding gasoline still rose only 10 basis points, while core merchandise margins fell 11 basis points, so the core business is giving up margin. The 'timing effect' label is management's framing, not a demonstrated reversal. On refunds, the bull concedes they are not durable, yet reported 2026 net income still benefited from $174 million booked against merchandise costs, which flatters the year regardless of where the money goes next. Membership renewal of 92.3% is in the U.S. and Canada only; worldwide renewal is 89.8%, and the filing says international growth and online sign-ups renew at lower rates. Finally, concentration remains severe: the U.S. and Canada generate 86% and 83% of net sales and operating income, and California is 26% of U.S. sales.

claims.claim: Core merchandise margins declined, so the mix-shift explanation does not fully cover margin pressure in the core business.
claims.quote: offset by an 11 basis point decrease in core merchandise categories

claims.claim: Worldwide renewal is lower than the headline U.S. and Canada figure the bull cited.
claims.quote: member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide

claims.claim: Earnings depend heavily on the U.S. and Canada, with California a large single exposure.
claims.quote: Within the U.S., we are highly dependent on our California operations, which comprised 26% of U.S. net sales in 2026.

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes from the filing, so evidence is comparable. The bull effectively reframes the refunds as pass-through and defends ex-gasoline comparable growth, while the bear rightly notes the 8%-to-7% deceleration, the 89.8% worldwide renewal figure, and the $174 million refund benefit to reported income. Neither side fully resolves the other's strongest point, so the debate is roughly even.
